chunks: Ways to throttle performance. The question: What can you do to throttle performance?
Throttling means deliberately slowing a chip so it stays within limits on temperature, power, current or battery.
The main method is to lower the voltage and clock speed together, which is called DVFS.
Other methods are stopping the clock for part of the time, limiting how many instructions run per clock tick, switching off some cores, and capping memory traffic.
Sensors trigger it when readings pass set thresholds.
Picture driving up a long hill on a hot day. The engine overheats if you keep flooring it.
Easing off the accelerator and taking the hill at a steady, slower pace is the efficient fix.
Driving flat out and then coasting in neutral every few seconds also cools the engine, but it wastes fuel.
At first the engine can still go hard for a while before the gauge climbs, because it takes time to heat up.
A throttling system is a closed loop.
Sensors feed a controller that picks one or more actuators; the thermal response closes the loop with a delay of seconds, which is why gain, hysteresis and layering matter.
Throttling: deliberately reducing performance to stay within limits. P-state: one voltage and frequency pair that the chip can run at.
DVFS: moving between P-states by changing voltage and frequency together. Clock modulation: stopping the clock for a fraction of the time, so average speed drops.
Hysteresis: using a different temperature to start throttling than to stop it, so the chip does not flip back and forth.
Thermal time constant: the seconds it takes temperature to respond when power changes.
A chip uses 96. 8 watts at 4 gigahertz and 1. 1 volts, and the limit calls for half the power, 48. 4 watts.
Stopping the clock half the time halves the power and also halves the speed, to 50%. DVFS instead settles at about 2. 62 gigahertz and 0. 96 volts.
Power scales with voltage squared times frequency, so that gives 96. 8 times (0. 96 over 1. 1) squared times (2. 62 over 4) about 48 watts at about 65% of the speed.
Lowering voltage as well gives more speed for the same power. That is the whole idea.
"The main throttle is DVFS: lower voltage and frequency together, which cuts power by roughly V squared times f.

Faster, cruder options are clock modulation, which gates the clock for some fraction of cycles, and microarchitectural throttling of fetch and issue width; coarser ones park cores or cap memory and accelerator bandwidth.
Triggers are temperature, power or current limits, with hysteresis. DVFS is the most efficient; clock gating at fixed voltage is the emergency tool."
